title: The Gift of Divine Life: The Promise of the Nicene Creed.
author: Godfrey I.K
content: Life is a gift before it is a journey.
Before we think, speak, or act, we receive. Every breath enters our lungs unearned. Every sunrise arrives without our command. Every heartbeat testifies to a life sustained by Another.

The deepest gift God offers is not merely existence, but participation in His own divine life. From the beginning, humanity was created for communion with God. The story of salvation is the story of God drawing His people into that communion through Jesus Christ.
The Nicene Creed emerged from this great mystery. It was not born from a desire to win an argument, but from a longing to preserve the truth of the God who gives Himself to us.
The Search for Understanding
Long before bishops gathered in Nicaea, believers gathered around the Scriptures.

They heard the opening words of John's Gospel proclaimed: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." They listened as Jesus declared: "I and the Father are one." They baptised in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Yet a profound question remained: "Who exactly is Jesus?" Was He merely the greatest of God's creatures? Or was He truly and eternally God, sharing the very life of the Father?
This question touched the very heart of Christian faith.
A theological dispute arose in Alexandria.

Arius, a respected presbyter, sought to protect the uniqueness and supremacy of God the Father. Drawing from passages such as Deuteronomy 6:4, John 14:28, and Colossians 1:15, he argued that the Son was brought into existence by the Father's will. Though exalted above all creation, the Son was not eternal in the same way as the Father.
Others, led by Archbishop Alexander, believed that this understanding could not fully account for the witness of Scripture.

They pointed to passages such as: John 1:1, where the "Word is called God."; John 17:5, where "Christ speaks of glory shared with the Father before the world existed."; Hebrews 1:3, where the Son is described as the "exact representation of God's being." and John 14:9, where Jesus declares that "whoever has seen Him has seen the Father."

For Alexander and those who shared his conviction, salvation itself was at stake. If Christ were merely a creature, how could He fully reveal God? If Christ were not truly divine, how could humanity be united to God through Him?
The debate was not simply about language. It was about the very nature of salvation.
The First Council of Nicaea

In AD 325, Emperor Constantine convened a council in the city of Nicaea. Bishops travelled from across the Christian world. Historical records indicate that between 250 and 318 bishops attended, most from the eastern provinces, while representatives also came from the western Church.

They did not gather merely as scholars. Many came bearing the memories of persecution. Some carried scars received for confessing Christ during earlier Roman persecutions. Together they listened to Scripture. Together they prayed. Together they debated. Together they sought to express faithfully the apostolic faith they had received.
The council's central concern was the question that echoes through every generation: "Who is Jesus Christ?"

Truth is often refined in seasons of tension. Scripture itself bears witness to God's people wrestling with difficult questions while seeking His guidance. Strong convictions were expressed. Passages were examined. Arguments were tested. Yet beyond every disagreement stood a greater reality: "God had not abandoned His people." The Holy Spirit who inspired the Scriptures continued to lead believers toward a deeper understanding of the faith entrusted to them.
Human voices filled the council chamber, but divine grace remained the quiet strength holding the Church together.

The council affirmed that the Son is homoousios, "of the same substance" as the Father. This single expression sought to safeguard a profound truth: "Jesus Christ is not merely like God." Jesus Christ truly shares the divine nature.
The creed that emerged from Nicaea was more than a theological statement. It was a gift. A gift preserving the Church's confession that the eternal Son reveals the Father perfectly.

"I believe in one God, the Father Almighty, Maker of heaven and earth... And in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God... And was crucified also for us under Pontius Pilate... And the third day He rose again... And I believe in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and Giver of life.. And I look for the resurrection of the dead, and the life of the world to come. Amen."
The Nicene Creed became a lamp handed from generation to generation, helping Christians recognise the face of the One they worship.
Why does this matter today?
Because the creed speaks of more than doctrine. It speaks of relationship.

The Son became human so that humanity might share in the life of God. The writer of Hebrews presents Christ as our great High Priest, the One who entered fully into our condition and offered Himself for our salvation. Through His self-giving sacrifice, the barrier between humanity and God is removed.
The question of Nicaea is therefore not an abstract question. It is deeply personal.
If Jesus is truly the eternal Son of God, then His invitation carries infinite depth. If He reveals the Father perfectly, then to know Christ is to know the heart of God.

Bartimaeus recognised something many others overlooked. Though physically blind, he perceived something profound about Jesus. He called out to Him as the promised Son of David. And when his sight was restored, it was not merely a miracle. It was a sign. The opening of blind eyes points to God's saving presence. The greatest blindness is not of the eyes but of the heart.

The greatest sight is to recognise who Christ truly is. The Nicene Creed invites us into that vision. Not merely to understand Christ. But to behold Him. Not merely to speak words about God. But to receive the life God offers through His Son.

The bishops at Nicaea answered a question that every generation must answer again: "Who is Jesus?" Not only in books. Not only in churches. Not only in councils. But within the silent sanctuary of the heart.
The God confessed in the Nicene Creed remains present today. The Father continues to create and sustain. The Son continues to reveal and redeem. The Holy Spirit continues to give life.
The promise of the Creed is therefore not simply correct belief. Its deeper promise is participation in divine life.
Prayer
Holy Lord, Source of life and eternal love,
Thank You for revealing Yourself through Your Son, Jesus Christ. Open the eyes of my heart that I may see beyond words and doctrines to the living reality of Your presence.
When doubts arise, strengthen my faith. When confusion surrounds me, guide me into Your truth.
As generations before me confessed Your name, help me to trust in the One who is eternally with the Father and who came to draw humanity into divine communion.
May every breath remind me that life is Your gift. May every day draw me deeper into Your love.
Through Christ our Lord.
Amen.
